articles.title: 'Nothing changes the ultimate thematic': Mining expert's optimistic take on lithium and copper - Stockhead
articles.summary: 'Nothing changes the ultimate thematic': Mining expert's optimistic take on lithium and copper  Stockhead
articles.full_text:
- Argonaut remains positive on lithium despite a rocky few months for the battery metal
- Head of research Hayden Bairstow says seasonal lull doesn’t change the ultimate thematic
- Broker also lifts long-term copper price 9%, with Kantra Copper one of its top producer picks
Lithium stocks have been hammered since May, when a burgeoning rebound in both chemical and spodumene prices began to deflate.
Despite pulling much higher prices than it did a year ago and approving an expansion that will see it ramp up spodumene production to ~780,000tpa by early next decade, Kathleen Valley owner Liontown (ASX:LTR) shares are down 22% on 12 months ago.
Market leader PLS Group (ASX:PLS) is up 37% over that horizon, but 14% down YTD despite resuming dividend payments this year.
Mineral Resources (ASX:MIN), IGO (ASX:IGO), Core Lithium (ASX:CXO) and Elevra Lithium (ASX:ELV) have hit similar turbulence.
The spot prices for both lithium carbonate and spodumene have taken a 25% hit in the past month in a seasonally weak period for lithium demand heading into China’s Golden Week holiday. They now run below US$1700/t.
But looking through the recent volatility, Argonaut’s executive director and head of research Hayden Bairstow says the fundamentals remain positive for the sector.
He believes spodumene, after trading within a US$2000-3000/t range for most of 2026, will move between US$1800-2500/t in the months ahead, predicting the market will shift regularly through cyclical troughs and peaks for the rest of the decade.
Argonaut tips average spod prices will rise from US$1570/t in FY26 to US$2250/t this year, US$2250t in FY28, US$2025/t in FY29, US$2169t in FY30 and US$2498/t in FY31.
“Everyone seems to forget that demand is seasonal,” Bairstow told Stockhead.
“And that’s what we’re seeing now. You get weakness into the Golden Week, which is this week.
“China starts trading again on Friday and we’ll be back into normality really.
“I think there’s always seasonality in this stuff and prices get too high, and there’s an element of demand destruction at points, but nothing that really changes the ultimate thematic.”
Two demand sources
There are now two main demand sources for lithium.
The first is electric vehicles – sales of which rose 5% YoY by the end of August amid a shift from consumers to avoid spiking fuel prices during the Iran War.
The other is battery storage, which Bairstow called in April last year as a positive tailwind for lithium.
As it transpired, the rush in big battery installations pushed the lithium market into a deficit far earlier than commodity forecasters predicted.
Lithium demand from battery energy storage systems, or BESS, ran 51% higher in 2025 according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.
Bairstow says BESS demand though has come in spikes, contributing to market volatility.
“If you look at the data that has been put out, December last year there was a massive spike, which caused the turnaround in lithium to begin with. That was all largely China,” he said.
“June this year was all Saudi Arabia. There (have) been quarters where Australia’s been a big contributor. It’s not a China EV story where you’re going from 10% market share to 50% and you can just see the pattern emerging.
“It’s a little bit up and down. There’ll months where not much happens and then there’ll be another government spending program in whatever country and we’ll get another huge sort of swathe of battery demand out of whatever grid’s being built out across the globe.
“So it’ll be a bit more lumpy, and that’s why I think the price will be more volatile.”
But on the other side of the equation, supply is not matching the increase in demand. A lot of faith is being placed in Argentina, which Bairstow believes will ‘disappoint’.
Against that backdrop he says lithium producers will look “extremely cheap” should prices head back towards US$2000/t.
With a dearth of new projects in the pipeline, that makes advanced developers like Wildcat Resources (ASX:WC8) and PMET Resources (ASX:PMT) attractive, Bairstow said.
“They’re the two that are going to get into production this decade,” he said.
“Q2 and Whiterock’s pretty new and these things are much longer dated. Whereas Wildcat can probably make the development decision late this year or early next year and get into development for two years and start producing.
“PMET is probably a year later than that based on their approvals process.
“I think most investors will look three years out and both of those could potentially be producing within that three-year timeline, which is why I think they’ll get more and more attention.”
Core and Liontown are Argonaut’s producer picks.
Copper lift
Bairstow has also upped Argonaut’s copper forecasts, lifting its FY29 price 8% to US$6.98/lb, equivalent to around US$15,400/t.
Argonaut’s long-term copper price is up 9% to US$6/lb (US$13,200/t).
“The fundamental backdrop for copper continues to improve. Data centre and AI demand continues to grab headlines, while copper supply in Chile remains under pressure and stockpiling in the US has further tightened the market,” Bairstow said in a note last week.
On the supply side, he noted that copper production from the world’s largest producing nation Chile had declined more than 20% in the past four years despite rising prices.
That has driven price target increases across a number of stocks, most of which boast big total shareholder returns if they meet Argonaut’s valuations.
It rates Jervois project developer KGL Resources (ASX:KGL) as having 224% upside, with Zambian proponent Prospect Resources (ASX:PSC) boasting 180% upside and Canadian market darling FireFly Metals (ASX:FFM) with 150% upside.
Among Bairstow’s key picks is Kantra Copper (ASX:KAN), which owns the Kanmantoo mine in the Adelaide Hills of South Australia.
It has a $2.40 price target, more than double the miner’s current price, representing the largest TSR in Argonaut’s copper producer coverage should it hit those levels.
Its Kanmantoo mine is expected to produce 12,750-14,000t of copper metal this year, with lower costs and higher prices helping the junior to $34.8m in EBITDA for the first half, eclipsing the $26m in EBITDA Kantra made for the whole of 2025.
A new growth leg has been established as well via a farm-in agreement to potentially develop Havilah Resources’ (ASX:HAV) Mutooroo project near Broken Hill, since renamed Coburn.
“It’s just an unknown story, right?” Bairstow told Stockhead.
“It was Hillgrove, it’s now Kantra. They’ve got this new project, the old Mutooroo, which is now called Coburn.
“There’s a lot of potential there that I just don’t think that the market really understands or recognises and that’s where the upside can come from. So as they become better known over time, I think they’ll get more of a rerate.
“We’ve seen it with AIC Mines (ASX:A1M) and these things have all gone pretty hard, but they’re all 25-30,000 tonne a year copper miners. Kantra can get to that with (Coburn).
“So that would mean that they’re in that ballpark and they’re capped at $200m. All those other things are capped at $700m.”
Argonaut also upped its long-term zinc price 4% to US$1.40/lb.

articles.title: OPEC+ To Keep Oil Quotas Unchanged In November As Iran War Continues To Impact Output, Keeping Crude Prices On The Boil: Report - Stocktwits
articles.summary: OPEC+ To Keep Oil Quotas Unchanged In November As Iran War Continues To Impact Output, Keeping Crude Prices On The Boil: Report  Stocktwits
articles.full_text:
OPEC+ is reportedly set to keep oil production quotas unchanged in November as the Iran war continues to disrupt output across the Persian Gulf.
The decision comes as crude prices push back toward $100 a barrel and diesel prices hit records, with the supply shock prompting the Group of Seven to coordinate a massive emergency stock release.
The seven-member OPEC+ subgroup led by Saudi Arabia and Russia has reached an agreement in principle to keep November production targets unchanged, delegates told Bloomberg ahead of Sunday’s video conference, where the decision is expected to be finalized.
The move would follow the group’s existing production roadmap. OPEC+ had already signaled that it would pause further quota increases through the end of 2026, after implementing modest production increases during the six months through August.
The latest increases had largely been symbolic in terms of actual market supply, with the Iran war disrupting production and exports across the Persian Gulf.
The conflict has left output from major OPEC producers, including Saudi Arabia, Iraq and Kuwait, significantly below prewar levels, limiting the practical impact of the group’s quota decisions.
OPEC+ is expected to settle its broader 2027 production policy at a full ministerial meeting in November.
The OPEC+ decision comes as governments move to counter the growing fuel-supply squeeze.
President Donald Trump said that the U.S. will not impose a proposed diesel export ban after the “Group of Seven” nations agreed to coordinate the release of 100 million barrels of crude oil and petroleum products from emergency reserves.
The release will begin immediately and run for four months, with the G7 saying a “substantial” amount of diesel will reach the market during the first 20 days.
Trump had repeatedly floated restricting U.S. diesel exports as European fuel supplies came under pressure following disruptions to Gulf production.
“Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately,” Trump said in a Truth Social post.
The G7 also committed to avoiding energy and energy-product export restrictions between member nations and urged other oil-producing countries to avoid measures that could further tighten global supplies.
The group said it will coordinate the releases through the International Energy Agency and could discuss additional diesel releases if market conditions deteriorate further.
The emergency action follows the IEA's record 400-million-barrel coordinated stock release in March, underscoring the scale of the supply shock facing global energy markets.
Crude oil prices were mixed last week, with the U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures expiring in November falling 1.41% to $91.26 a barrel after a 3.82% fall the week before. However, Brent crude futures expiring in December rose 3.47% this week, hovering around $102.72 a barrel after a 0.46% increase the week before.
The United States Oil Fund ETF (USO) declined about 2% on Friday, while the ProShares Ultra Bloomberg Crude Oil ETF (UCO) fell about 0.4%.
During the after-hours session on Friday, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), which tracks the S&P 500 index, rose 0.03%; the Invesco QQQ Trust ETF (QQQ) was flat; and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) rose 0.12%. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits toward the S&P 500 ETF was in the ‘extremely bullish’ territory at the time of writing.

Arbitrum (ARB) extended its one-week drop after emergency action by the network’s Security Council. The token traded in the red on Sunday, down about 12% in seven days.
In a report on the action, the Arbitrum Foundation said the Council paused new Stylus contract activations on Arbitrum One and Nova on Thursday. It moved at 11:30 a.m. ET. Live contracts continue to run. None of them mature before Aug. 20, 2027, the Foundation said.
The pause applies to new contracts and apps that require a new activation to update. The Foundation said it is going after hand-built WebAssembly programs that circumvent the normal Stylus toolchain. It said such AI-assisted tools have made attacks on those programs more sophisticated.
Known bugs in Stylus mostly threaten the chain’s uptime, such as denial-of-service attacks. The Foundation said no attack that would allow someone to steal user funds has been found so far.
While ARB has been up over 47% in the past month, Arbitrum’s price was down over 0.6% over the past 24 hours, defying broader market strength as Bitcoin's price climbed past $85,000. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment around ARB remained in the ‘bearish’ zone with chatter at ‘low’ levels over the last day.
The same action allowed for a safety net to materialize in the BoLD dispute mechanism on Arbitrum One. Any party can trigger it in situations when two contradictory responses are accepted with one proof. Meanwhile, Arbitrum One will remain operational, the Foundation said.
Unconfirmed withdrawals would have to wait until the settlement resumes. The foundation added that it will work with the Arbitrum Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) on when and how to reopen new activations. It said the community still sees value in Stylus.
However, Arbitrum’s ecosystem remains strong. Arbitrum reported on Thursday that its monthly revenue had increased by about five times. Licensing fees brought in $4.75 million, or about 87% of the total, while transaction fees added about $507,000, and treasury income contributed about $181,000. The network also said it had processed 1.5 billion new transactions so far this year.
The Arbitrum Foundation said in a first-half report published Sept. 2 that income of $6.19 million accrued to the ArbitrumDAO in the six months to June 30. In mid-September, Geoff Kendrick of Standard Chartered predicted Arbitrum’s monthly revenue could reach approximately $5 million in September at the current run rate, calling it "hugely undervalued”.
ARB’s price has been up over 7% so far this year, but down over 53% in the last 12 months.

Tesla Inc. (TSLA) may be delivering stronger-than-expected vehicle numbers, but The Future Fund managing partner Gary Black says the bigger question is whether Elon Musk’s company can close the widening gap with Alphabet Inc.’s (GOOG, GOOGL) Waymo in autonomous driving.
In a post on X, Black pointed to Tesla’s recent delivery strength while highlighting a much tougher challenge ahead, which is scaling unsupervised autonomy fast enough to catch competitors already operating driverless vehicles across multiple U.S. markets.
Tesla shares closed nearly 5% higher on Friday, while Alphabet’s Class A shares gained nearly 2%.
Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in the third quarter (Q3), beating the company-compiled analyst consensus of 461,974 and marking its second consecutive major delivery beat.
Black noted that Q3 deliveries fell just 2% year-over-year despite the comparison with Tesla’s record Q3 last year, when the $7,500 EV tax credit was nearing expiration.
That followed Tesla’s Q2 delivery blowout, when the company delivered roughly 480,000 vehicles against Wall Street expectations of about 406,000.
“That says it all,” Black said of Tesla’s latest delivery performance. But with demand showing signs of stabilization, Black argued that investors are increasingly looking beyond vehicle sales.
Black said that the investor focus is now shifting to Tesla’s ability to scale unsupervised autonomy, an area where he says the company’s generalized Full Self-Driving (FSD) technology is “clearly superior” to competitors. The problem, he argues, is execution.
Black said Tesla’s scale-up has “fallen far short of management’s guidance,” pointing to previous targets for unsupervised autonomy without safety drivers in eight to 10 metro areas by the end of 2025.
Tesla currently has unsupervised autonomy approved for use in six U.S. metros — Austin, Dallas and Houston in Texas, plus Miami, Orlando and Tampa in Florida.
The San Francisco Bay Area is next on deck, while Las Vegas has been approved for a permit but is not yet live.
Tesla’s current guidance calls for unsupervised autonomous miles to compound at more than 10% per week.
Black also compared Tesla’s robotaxi coverage with the service offered by Waymo.
He highlighted that Waymo has been authorized for public fully driverless rides in 15 U.S. metros, including Phoenix, the Bay Area, Los Angeles, San Diego, Austin, Dallas, Houston, San Antonio, Atlanta, Miami, Orlando, Tampa, Denver, Nashville and Las Vegas.
The company operates roughly 4,000-plus driverless vehicles nationwide, according to Black.
Tesla, meanwhile, had about 589 vehicles registered in Texas as fully autonomous as of Oct. 2, including 420 Model Ys and 169 Cybercabs, Black said, while adding that this makes autonomy the critical test for Tesla from here.

articles.title: Critical Minerals: 5 Smart Bets in a Powerful New Race - Global Brands Magazine
articles.summary: Critical Minerals: 5 Smart Bets in a Powerful New Race  Global Brands Magazine
articles.full_text:
Every electric car, wind turbine, data centre and smartphone rests on a short list of raw materials that most people never think about. Critical minerals, the group that includes lithium, copper, cobalt, nickel, graphite and the rare earths, have quietly become some of the most strategically important commodities on the planet. In 2026 the race to secure them has moved from mining conferences into corporate boardrooms.
The reason is demand. According to the International Energy Agency, lithium demand is projected to rise roughly 353% between 2024 and 2040, while graphite demand could climb about 131%. Global battery demand alone grew more than 35% in 2025, passing 1.5 terawatt-hours, with grid-scale storage joining electric vehicles as a major pull. These are not niche materials any more. They are the building blocks of the electrified economy.
Why critical minerals matter now
The shift is being driven by three overlapping trends. Electric vehicles need large batteries, and batteries need lithium, nickel, cobalt and graphite. Electricity grids are expanding and modernising, which takes enormous quantities of copper. And the motors, magnets and electronics inside everything from wind turbines to robots depend on rare earth elements. Add fast-growing demand for computing power, and the pressure on supply only builds.
For companies, that turns raw materials into a competitive issue. A carmaker without secure battery materials cannot promise buyers a steady supply. An electronics firm exposed to a single source of rare earths carries a risk it may not fully understand. What used to be a purchasing detail is now a question of corporate resilience.
A concentrated supply chain
The awkward truth about critical minerals is that supply is heavily concentrated, especially in the refining stage where raw ore becomes usable material. The IEA notes that for copper, lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite and rare earths, the combined market share of the top three refining nations rose to about 86% in 2024, up from around 82% in 2020. Battery recycling capacity is even more concentrated, with one country accounting for roughly 90% of material recovery capacity.
| Mineral | Projected demand growth (2024-2040) | 
|---|---|
| Lithium | ~+353% | 
| Graphite | ~+131% | 
| Copper, nickel, rare earths | Strong, steady growth | 
| Global battery demand (2025) | +35% year on year, past 1.5 TWh | 
Concentration is not a moral judgement, it is a business risk. When most of the world’s refining or recycling sits in a few places, a single disruption, whether weather, technical or logistical, can ripple through every industry that depends on the output. That is why diversification has become a strategic priority for so many companies at once.
The companies that treat critical minerals as an afterthought today are the ones most likely to be caught short tomorrow.
The recycling opportunity
One of the most promising responses is recycling. Today, average recycling rates across key energy minerals sit at roughly 10%, but the IEA expects that to climb towards 20% by 2040 under current policies, with cobalt and copper further ahead. Recovering minerals from used batteries and scrap could become a meaningful second source of supply, and a business in its own right, though it needs sustained investment in collection and processing to reach its potential.
The scale of investment required is large. Diversifying magnet rare earth supply chains alone would take around $60 billion over the next decade, by IEA estimates. That is capital looking for a return, which is exactly why miners, manufacturers and investors are circling the sector.
Recycling has a second benefit beyond supply. Recovering critical minerals from old devices and batteries uses far less energy and water than digging fresh ore, which appeals to companies under pressure to shrink their environmental footprint. It also keeps valuable material inside the economies that already own it, rather than shipping it out as waste and buying it back later as finished product. For brands that want a supply story they can stand behind, a credible recycling loop is becoming a genuine advantage.
Copper, the quiet giant
Lithium and rare earths grab the headlines, but copper may be the most important critical mineral of all, because almost nothing electrifies without it. Every electric car, charging point, solar farm, wind turbine and data centre needs large amounts of copper wiring, and demand keeps climbing as grids expand to carry more power. Unlike some exotic materials, copper is mined and used at massive scale, which makes even small imbalances between supply and demand ripple widely through prices.
New copper mines take a long time to bring online, often a decade or more from discovery to production. That lag is exactly why analysts worry about a squeeze later this decade, as demand from electrification and computing runs ahead of new supply. For companies planning long-lived investments, from carmakers to utilities, copper is no longer something to take for granted. It is a strategic input to be secured well in advance.
The same pattern shows up across the group. Building a new mine, refinery or recycling plant is slow and capital-intensive, while demand can shift quickly. That mismatch between fast demand and slow supply is the core tension in critical minerals, and it is why the topic has jumped up the corporate agenda rather than staying in the commodities pages.
How companies are securing critical minerals
The corporate playbook is taking shape. Manufacturers are signing long-term offtake deals directly with miners, sometimes years before a mine opens, to lock in supply. Some are investing in mining and refining projects themselves rather than relying on the open market. Others are building recycling operations to create a domestic loop. And a wave of consolidation is under way, as shown by high-profile talks such as those we covered between Glencore and Rio Tinto.
Investment is following the demand. Mining and refining projects that struggled to raise money a few years ago are attracting fresh capital, and specialist funds have sprung up to back critical minerals ventures from exploration through to recycling. Governments and large manufacturers are co-investing too, sharing the risk of building supply that may take years to come good. For patient investors, the appeal is a rare combination of structural demand growth and genuine scarcity, though the sector carries real risks around cost overruns, permitting and price swings.
The corporate lesson is to map exposure before it becomes a crisis. That means knowing which critical minerals sit inside your products, where they are refined, and what would happen if a single source went offline. Firms that can answer those questions calmly are in a far stronger position than those discovering the answer during a shortage. Increasingly, that mapping is being done at board level, alongside the traditional risks of currency, cyber and demand.
The through-line connects to stories GBM has followed elsewhere, from the race to commercialise solid-state batteries to the business of carbon capture and the wider return of hardware. All of them depend, in the end, on getting enough of the right materials at a price that works. Critical minerals have become the quiet foundation of the next industrial era, and the companies treating them as a strategic priority are the ones building on solid ground. The agreement marks a significant step for the rare earths developer, whose largest shareholder is Rinehart’s Hancock Prospecting, which holds a 17.5% stake.
Under the five-year agreement, Arafura will supply 850 tonnes a year of neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide once Nolans reaches full production, up from the 500 tonnes originally proposed under a term sheet signed in May.
The agreement also includes heavy rare earths and provides an option for a further two-year extension by mutual consent.
US critical minerals supply chain connection
The unnamed trading partner participates in the US government's Project Vault initiative, which is designed to strengthen critical minerals supply chains and improve access to materials essential for American manufacturers.
The agreement positions Arafura to supply rare earth materials into a market increasingly focused on securing alternative sources of critical minerals.
Pricing will be denominated in US dollars and linked to an independent seaborne price index, such as those published by Benchmark Minerals Intelligence or S&P Global Platts.
Further offtake negotiations continue
Arafura continues to negotiate with other potential customers as it progresses development of the Nolans Project, which is expected to produce rare earth materials used in permanent magnets for electric vehicles, wind turbines and other advanced technologies.
The company has also indicated it will no longer routinely disclose the identities of potential offtake counterparties unless required, citing the need to protect commercially sensitive negotiations.

articles.title: The Race for Lithium Is Becoming a Race for Water - Inside Climate News
articles.summary: The Race for Lithium Is Becoming a Race for Water  Inside Climate News
articles.full_text:
This investigation was reported in a collaboration between Inside Climate News and Columbia Journalism Investigations.
CALIPATRIA, Calif.—On a border-town road surrounded by alfalfa and grain fields, William Cooper stopped before a dusty, vacant lot. Its owner, he said, is one of many investors drawn to the arid Imperial Valley by a critical mineral propelling the green energy transition.
“They buy it up and leave it, just waiting for the opportunity,” Cooper said of the land investors.
Now, with each gust of desert wind, dust drifts from the lot into the yards of two adjacent schools. Often, the buildings disappear behind a haze and the schoolchildren gasp for air, said Cooper, who moved here from San Diego years ago.
The pollution adds to a litany of burdens plaguing one of the nation’s poorest areas. And it hints at a new pressure reshaping the area’s future: a lithium deposit buried beneath a nearby lake called the Salton Sea—the mother lode for prospectors rushing to extract this key ingredient for the batteries that power electric vehicles.
Companies are racing to draw out lithium from brine bubbling below the Salton Sea. With hefty government support, developers say they will create “the most sustainable lithium and power project in the world,” bringing hundreds of jobs and billions of dollars here.
In Calipatria’s county, Imperial, local officials greenlit two mines and launched an ambitious proposal to use direct lithium extraction, a fledgling technology touted as a cleaner alternative than traditional lithium mining. Company executives and government officials alike promise to transform Imperial Valley into a renewable-energy hub—what they call “the next Silicon Valley.”
These lithium ventures are among 100 proposed mining projects advancing through the permitting pipeline in the country today, as the U.S. ramps up critical-mineral production. By 2030, at least half dozen new mines are expected to extract lithium, with another 13 soon to follow, an investigation by Columbia Journalism Investigations and Inside Climate News has found. Most are concentrated in the dry Southwest.
Using corporate filings and other records collected by the financial firm S&P Global, the news organizations identified roughly 540 proposed lithium mines worldwide, as well as the companies and investors behind them. The first-of-its-kind dataset offers a window into just who controls America’s lithium rush—from global mining conglomerates and smaller explorations firms, many based in Australia and Canada, to powerful American financial institutions that dominate the sector’s funding network.
Nearly two-thirds of the proposed and developing mines in the U.S. bump up against some of the nation’s most socially and economically vulnerable communities, according to an analysis by Columbia Journalism Investigations and Inside Climate News of demographic measures like income, age and race. Topping that list is Imperial County, an area of mostly Hispanic residents that has severe unemployment rates, low schooling levels and crowded housing conditions.
Interviews with dozens of residents, advocates, government officials and company executives and visits to four states reveal the stark tension in the energy transition: Who gets to define “clean”? And who has to live with the impacts of mining needed to build cars that don’t foul the air?
In Imperial County, where lush farms dominate an otherwise parched landscape, rising heat and drought are colliding with the lithium industry’s water demands. Control over increasingly scarce water supplies determines who will benefit from lithium extraction and who will bear its costs. A small number of landowners whose water rights date back a century are set to profit, while many nearby residents struggle to pay the basic utility rate for clean drinking water.
Lax and inconsistent regulations leave these same residents with few enforceable economic, environmental and community protections.
James J.A. Blair, an associate professor of anthropology at California State Polytechnic University, Pomona, has studied lithium mining’s social impacts. Places like Calipatria already face significant inequities, he said, and lithium development that doesn’t attempt to mitigate them is likely to deepen those rifts. The mineral’s importance to the clean energy transition means its impacts on communities and the environment often receive little scrutiny, he added.
“They’re using lithium as a kind of loophole to make everything seem green,” Blair said.
Across the West, the lithium boom is on a collision course with climate-driven declines in rivers and aquifers. Federal data shows that almost all proposed or developing lithium projects are in counties where risk of drought is expected to rise sharply—much more so than in most of the nation. Nearly six in 10 are in places where drought is projected to cause some of the most severe impacts.
A recent study concludes that most lithium mining areas won’t have enough water by mid-century to meet the industry’s demands.
“Those regions are already water-stressed,” said co-author Jennifer Dunn, director of the Center for Engineering Sustainability and Resilience at Northwestern University. Adding lithium mining onto them without reducing water consumption across the board will make it extremely challenging for those mines to operate in the near future, not to mention meeting everyone’s water needs, she said. “As engineers, we can think of some technology solutions to cut water consumption, but the engineering is not going to get you over the hump in this case. It really has to be a local discussion about how we want to use water.”
In Amargosa Valley, Nevada, where wells are already running dry, residents feared that a lithium mining company’s proposed drilling would threaten their sole water supply. The high-poverty town sits in one of the state’s most climate-stressed counties. After the Biden administration paused mining in January 2025 to evaluate how to protect local water resources, the company scrapped its lithium plans. Hydrogen's value for energy security is rising, but the transition faces challenges
Projected potential production in 2030 fell 27% in a year
Japan supports price differences, China expands demand, and the U.S. ensures investment continuity
① An ecosystem caught in a vicious cycle just as it was getting started

④ There are stages to the clean hydrogen transition... Strategies of the U.S., China and Japan
⑤ "Korea is trapped in idealism... It needs to redesign a realistic pathway"
Korea is heavily dependent on energy imports. According to the Korea Energy Agency on October 12, the country's energy import dependency stood at 93.7% in 2024, based on preliminary figures. Countries that rely heavily on overseas sources for energy, like Korea, are more vulnerable to geopolitical shocks. That is because heavy dependence on specific suppliers and energy sources can shake industries and the economy as a whole.
Europe's dependence on Russian natural gas is a recent example that has once again underscored this risk. After Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, it sharply reduced pipeline gas supplies to Europe, driving up gas prices and triggering a severe energy crisis across the continent. In the Middle East, every outbreak of conflict raises concerns about supply disruptions involving major oil-producing countries and transit routes, including the Strait of Hormuz, adding to uncertainty in global oil prices and the world economy.
Hydrogen's strategic value is increasingly coming into focus from an energy security perspective. Its role goes beyond serving as an energy source for addressing the climate crisis and achieving carbon neutrality. The International Energy Agency (IEA) has said hydrogen can broaden the range of domestic energy sources countries use, reduce dependence on fossil fuel imports, and help diversify suppliers and supply routes. In particular, renewable-based hydrogen can be produced in regions beyond the major oil and gas-producing countries, helping to diversify suppliers.
However, hydrogen cannot solve an energy crisis immediately. According to the IEA, low-emissions hydrogen, including green hydrogen, which has substantially lower carbon emissions during production, is still more expensive than conventional fossil fuel-based hydrogen in most regions. Building infrastructure for large-scale production, storage and transportation also takes considerable time. It is also difficult for companies to commit to large-scale investment when demand has yet to reach sufficient levels. Although hydrogen is becoming increasingly important for energy security, significant barriers remain before it can become part of a functioning market.
In its Global Hydrogen Review 2026, released by the IEA in June, the agency estimated that low-emissions hydrogen projects announced with the aim of starting operations by 2030 have the potential to produce 27 million tonnes annually. That is 27% lower than the 37 million tonnes projected in last year's report. The decline reflects delays to some projects beyond 2030 and the temporary suspension or cancellation of others. High production costs and uncertain demand were also cited as major obstacles to moving projects forward. Global demand for low-emissions hydrogen last year was about 1 million tonnes, less than 1% of total hydrogen demand.
Nevertheless, major countries are refining their policies to reduce the costs and risks of the transition as they seek to develop low-emissions hydrogen markets over the long term. Environmental imperatives such as carbon neutrality alone are not enough to move the market. The IEA has also recommended that, rather than waiting for new sources of demand, countries should first transition industries that already use hydrogen, such as refining and chemicals, to low-emissions hydrogen; provide support to narrow the initial price gap; and establish a predictable policy framework over the long term. Ultimately, the key is how smoothly countries can manage the transition from conventional fossil fuel-based hydrogen to low-emissions hydrogen.
Japan has pursued hydrogen-related technology development and policies for more than 50 years as part of its energy security strategy, following the oil shocks of the 1970s. Japan's energy self-sufficiency rate was 15.3% in 2023, the lowest among the Group of Seven (G7) countries. Industry observers in Korea and abroad broadly consider Japan to view hydrogen as a core pillar of its national energy strategy and to have maintained policy certainty and institutional consistency to support it. Its policies have also expanded in stages, from basic research and development (R&D) to demonstration projects and supply chain development, and more recently to market creation and encouraging private investment.
Notably, Japan has opted for a pragmatic approach rather than relying solely on an idealized green hydrogen pathway. Prioritizing a realistic transition and the development of initial demand, it is pursuing several immediately viable options in parallel, including blue hydrogen and ammonia co-firing. In particular, Japan sees ammonia co-firing at existing thermal power plants as a practical way to create large-scale demand immediately without investing in new infrastructure, while also reducing carbon emissions from thermal power generation. This contrasts with Korea, which has excluded coal-ammonia co-firing from its clean hydrogen power generation auction market starting this year.
Japan also operates a contract-for-difference (CfD)-style scheme under the Hydrogen Society Promotion Act, which compensates for the price difference between low-carbon hydrogen and conventional fuels and feedstocks for 15 years. The government also supports supply chain development, including storage and transportation, as well as policy financing, sharing the risks associated with prices and investment. The strategy is to bridge the demand gap until green hydrogen infrastructure matures and realize a "hydrogen society" in stages.
China is developing its market with the aim of building a diversified hydrogen use ecosystem by 2035. Its Hydrogen Energy Comprehensive Application Pilot Program, announced in March, seeks to expand hydrogen use beyond fuel cell vehicles into industries such as steel and chemicals. It also calls for the gradual replacement of fossil fuel-based hydrogen with renewable-based hydrogen in industries that consume large amounts of hydrogen, such as refining and coal chemicals.
Support for creating demand is also designed to reward results. Rather than providing uniform subsidies from the central government, China is applying a performance-based approach that varies support according to results, such as the actual volume of hydrogen used and its application in products. Under the program, each city cluster can receive up to 1.6 billion yuan (about 320 billion won) over four years. The goal is to expand large-scale hydrogen use across city clusters by 2030 and reduce the average end-user price of hydrogen to no more than 25 yuan (about 5,000 won) per kilogram.
Even when hydrogen policies are pursued over the long term, specific measures can be adjusted in response to changes in government or market conditions. The United States is a case in point. In 2022, the administration of then-U.S. President Joe Biden made clean hydrogen projects that began construction by the end of 2032 eligible for the production tax credit (45V) under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). The second Trump administration moved the deadline forward by five years, to the end of 2027, but retained the provision allowing projects that begin construction by the deadline to receive tax credits for up to 10 years after starting production.

The government is accelerating efforts to foster a domestic clean hydrogen ecosystem, including water electrolysis, but the initial market is developing slowly. Related companies that have completed technology development and demonstration are also hesitant to expand mass production and invest in facilities because sufficient demand has yet to emerge. To make clean hydrogen price-competitive, production needs to be scaled up to bring down its high production costs. But the vicious cycle seen in the existing hydrogen market continues: insufficient demand prevents the expansion of mass production, while high production costs in turn constrain demand.
Clean hydrogen refers to hydrogen whose production emits no more than 4 kg of greenhouse gases per 1 kg of hydrogen, measured in carbon dioxide equivalents. The government plans to shift the hydrogen supply structure away from a focus on gray hydrogen based on fossil fuels, such as byproduct hydrogen and hydrogen produced through reforming, and toward clean hydrogen. Green hydrogen, produced by splitting water through electrolysis using electricity from renewable energy, is a leading type of clean hydrogen. As the government seeks to foster green hydrogen as a key pillar of production, the importance of water electrolysis technology and related materials and components is bound to grow.
However, analysts say Korea still has a long way to go before green hydrogen becomes economically viable. According to the Hydrogen Economy Information Portal, as of October 12, the domestic production cost of green hydrogen stands at more than 20,000 won per kg. This is far above the government's 2019 target, set out in its hydrogen technology development roadmap, of 3,500 won per kg by 2030. High production costs are seen as a major factor limiting the expansion of green hydrogen demand and slowing market development.
Han Sangbeom, CEO of Boyas Energy, introduces the research facilities at the company’s headquarters in Geumcheon-gu, Seoul, on the 8th of last month. Photo by Choi Hogyeong.

Boyaseu Energy, a prospective hydrogen-specialized company developing water electrolysis catalysts, is also caught in this vicious cycle. Launched in 2022, the support program for prospective hydrogen-specialized companies helps small and midsize businesses in the hydrogen sector grow into hydrogen-specialized companies by supporting technology commercialization and the development of sales channels, among other things. It also aims to foster the hydrogen industry ecosystem. Boyaseu Energy has developed and pursued the commercialization of water electrolysis catalyst technology needed for the transition to clean hydrogen. After localizing iridium oxide (IrO₂) catalysts for proton exchange membrane (PEM) water electrolysis, it has supplied them to major domestic companies.
But the company is not moving ahead with full-scale mass production or expanding its production facilities, as it cannot expect large orders for now. When met at Boyaseu Energy's headquarters in Geumcheon-gu, Seoul, on September 8, CEO Han Sangbeom said, "There is no reason to invest in mass production under the current circumstances," adding, "Revenue comes when a market exists, but so far, it is not economically viable." The company is ready in terms of technology and production, but it is difficult to be confident that there will be enough demand to support them.
Han cited the reduced auction volume in the Clean Hydrogen Power Generation Market (CHPS) as one reason companies find it difficult to anticipate growing demand. Although the government has stated its intention to foster the clean hydrogen industry, the size of the power generation market that should underpin demand has shrunk considerably. This has left companies questioning whether the government is truly willing to grow the market. "The auction volume this year has been cut so sharply that it is less than 10% of what it was in the past," he said.
The Clean Hydrogen Power Generation Market cited by Han is one segment of the hydrogen power generation auction market, where electricity produced from hydrogen or hydrogen compounds is traded through competitive bidding. It is distinct from the General Hydrogen Power Generation Market (HPS). According to the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment and the Korea Power Exchange (KPX), the Clean Hydrogen Power Generation Market was first launched in 2024 with an auction volume of 6,500 GWh, but only 750.48 GWh was awarded. Last year, an auction for 3,000 GWh was announced but ultimately canceled. This year's auction volume has been set at 500 GWh, a decline of more than 90% from the first auction in 2024. Han said that in addition to high production costs, declining policy consistency and predictability make it difficult for companies to decide whether to scale up mass production and invest in facilities.
The problem is not limited to uncertainty in the demand market. There is also a shortage of large-scale projects that could move water electrolysis technology from demonstration to commercialization. To lower the cost of water electrolysis equipment, materials, and components, and establish a mass-production system, companies need to build up operational experience and increase production scale. But domestic demonstration projects remain at around 10 MW. One notable example is the Jeju green hydrogen production demonstration project. Initially planned at 12.5 MW when it began in 2022, it was ultimately scaled down to 9.7 MW, partly due to cuts to the government's research and development (R&D) budget.

The United States Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) held about 283 million barrels of oil at the end of September 2026, marking its lowest level since 1982. This significant drawdown reflects the reserve’s extensive use amid recent global tensions and market disruptions.
Rapid Withdrawals and Slow Refills
The SPR was built to provide swift emergency oil supplies, and it has proven capable of quick releases. However, replenishing these reserves is a gradual and costly process. Currently, the reserve is being refilled through a program where released barrels are repaid with interest, ranging from 18% to 28%, though some repayments are not expected until 2028. Even if all planned returns occur on schedule, the reserve is projected to only recover to about two-thirds of its operational capacity.
Background to the Reserve’s Decline
Established in 1975 in response to the Arab oil embargo, the SPR reached its peak inventory of 726.6 million barrels in 2009. It maintained near 695 million barrels for much of the 2010s. However, following Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Biden administration authorized the sale of 180 million barrels, which constitutes the largest sustained drawdown in the reserve’s history. This depletion continued despite an effort by the Department of Energy to repurchase 59 million barrels and legislative cancellations of mandated sales of 140 million barrels to stabilize the reserves.
By early 2026, the SPR stood at about 58% of its authorized capacity of 713.5 million barrels, just as geopolitical conflicts in the Middle East intensified, including U.S. and Israeli strikes near the Strait of Hormuz that disrupted tanker traffic.
Why the SPR Status Matters for Pakistan
Pakistan is highly dependent on global oil markets and sensitive to price volatility due to its import reliance for energy needs. The U.S. SPR’s depletion and slow refill pace can exacerbate global supply uncertainties and impact crude oil prices worldwide. Consequently, fluctuations in oil availability and costs can affect Pakistan’s fuel prices and economic stability, especially as global geopolitical tensions continue to heighten market risks.
Michael Kern, an energy analyst, noted, “Though the drawdown is alarming, the SPR’s role as a flexible emergency system means it was utilized as intended, but replenishment remains a challenge for future administrations.” With Congress allocating only $171 million for refills against an estimated $20 billion needed for a full recovery, the reserve’s status will continue to influence international energy markets.

The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve held just 283 million barrels of oil at the end of September, according to Reuters, the lowest level since October 1982, back when the reserve was still being filled for the first time.
It's a scary-looking number, and most of the coverage has treated it that way. But the barrel count is the easy part of this story. Oil came out of those Gulf Coast salt caverns fast, because that's exactly what the system was built to do. Getting it back in is slower, more expensive and more dependent on things nobody controls. And a good chunk of that work will land on whoever is running the Energy Department two or three years from now.
The Reserve Started This War Already Depleted
Congress created the SPR in 1975, after the Arab oil embargo showed how exposed an import-dependent America really was. The reserve peaked at 726.6 million barrels at the end of 2009 and spent most of the 2010s hovering around 695 million, according to EIA data.
Then came 2022. After Russia invaded Ukraine, the Biden administration sold 180 million barrels, which the Government Accountability Office calls the largest sustained drawdown in the reserve's history, according to an October Atlantic Council brief. By the end of 2023, the SPR was down to 354.7 million barrels.
The reserve never really recovered. DOE bought back about 59 million barrels, and Congress canceled 140 million barrels of previously mandated sales so the hole wouldn't get any deeper. Year-end stocks crept back to 413.5 million barrels in 2025. That's roughly a quarter of what came out in 2022.
So when U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28 shut down most tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the SPR went into the fight at about 415 million barrels, or 58% of its authorized capacity of 713.5 million. In March, the U.S. committed 172 million barrels to a 400-million-barrel release coordinated by the International Energy Agency, the largest joint stock release the agency has ever authorized.
A Loan, Not a Sale
This is where 2026 gets different, and where a lot of the coverage gets fuzzy.
In 2022, the oil was sold. It left the caverns and didn't come back unless someone later paid to replace it. This time, DOE is running the entire 172-million-barrel release as a series of exchanges. In plain terms, it's a loan. Companies borrow crude now and pay it back later, in barrels, with interest.
And the interest is steep. Winning bidders in the first round had to return 18% to 22% more oil than they borrowed, two to seven times the premium DOE required in its last exchange in 2021. Later rounds pushed premiums as high as 28%. DOE says its earlier exchanges averaged a 25% premium and has pitched the program as refilling the reserve at no cost to taxpayers. Reuters reported the premiums work out to about 40 million extra barrels.
Why would anyone take that deal? Backwardation, which is a fancy way of saying oil for delivery today costs a lot more than oil for delivery a year or two out. A trader borrows a barrel while it's worth, say, $100, sells it, and pays it back later, when the futures market says a barrel will be worth much less. As Employ America explained when the program launched, the premium is just the price of that trade.
In June, DOE offered 40 million barrels and awarded exactly 500,000, all of it to Vitol. Calendar spreads had collapsed, and the trade stopped making sense. When the futures curve flattens, nobody wants to borrow oil they'll have to pay back with interest, and the barrels just sit there.
DOE put those same 40 million barrels back on the table on Sept. 29, the final tranche of the U.S. commitment, with bids due Oct. 6 and deliveries set for November and December, Oilprice.com reported. Before that, roughly 133 million barrels had gone out under earlier exchanges.
The repayment side has its own catch. The math only works if those companies can actually find the barrels when they come due, in a market the Atlantic Council warns may not be able to spare them. And the timeline is long. Return windows in some of DOE's contracts run into late 2028, right up against the end of the current presidential term.
Nobody Agrees Where the Bottom Is
Here's what everyone actually wants to know: how low can the SPR go before something breaks?
The honest answer is that it depends on who you ask, and the range is enormous.
DOE says there's plenty of room left. The oil sits on top of salt water in the caverns, so as crude comes out, brine takes its place. Energy Department spokesman Ben Dietderich told CNBC the caverns are "always full" and that the only thing that changes is "the ratio of oil and water." The department's stated minimum to keep the system running is about 70 million barrels.
That's the physical floor, according to Siddharth Misra, a petroleum engineering professor at Texas A&M. It's the least oil you need to keep the extraction pipes sitting in crude instead of water. But Misra puts the practical floor at 250 million to 300 million barrels, and he told Fortune the industry should be "highly concerned about the integrity of the caverns" any time inventories drop below 300 million. Amos Hochstein, a former senior energy adviser to President Joe Biden, has said he doesn't know anyone who thinks the reserve can safely go much below 300 million.
In the Dallas Fed's third-quarter energy survey, the most common answer from executives, picked by 31% of them, put the practical floor between 100 million and 150 million barrels. Another 19% said 250 million to 300 million, according to Rigzone.
Congress set a floor of 252.4 million barrels, but it only applies to smaller drawdowns the energy secretary orders without a presidential emergency finding. Exchanges don't fall under it. DOE projects the reserve will bottom out around 243 million barrels once the full 172 million barrels are delivered, below the line that would stop a limited drawdown. And this isn't a new worry. A 1981 GAO report advised against releases below 250 million barrels except in a "very severe emergency."
Out at 1.4 Million Barrels a Day, Back In at a Trickle
The SPR was designed to release oil about six times faster than it can take it back in. Its design criteria call for a peak drawdown rate of 4.415 million barrels a day against a fill rate of 0.785 million. That made sense for a reserve built for emergencies. It makes refilling a slog.
And the real system can't hit those design numbers anyway. As of December 2025, the GAO found the SPR could draw down at 61% of its designed rate and fill at just 56%. Even during 2022, a release run at just over a fifth of the designed maximum still needed repeated emergency repairs to leaking pipes and pumps.
The Atlantic Council ran the numbers site by site. Bryan Mound, West Hackberry and Big Hill can each take in up to 225,000 barrels a day, but problems with West Hackberry's brine disposal wells have cut it to 112,000. Bayou Choctaw tops out at 110,000. Under perfect conditions, that's 672,000 barrels a day across the entire system, compared with the 1.4 million barrels a day that flowed out when the releases started in March.
At that pace, the 133 million barrels owed from the exchanges take at least 198 days to put back. Add the 20 million to 30 million barrels still owed from earlier congressional requirements, and the fill system has to run flat out for 220 to 230 days. The brief's authors say it could realistically take twice that, given what a sustained fill will do to aging infrastructure.
The infrastructure itself is part of the problem...
Three of the six caverns at Bayou Choctaw have only one drawdown left before they risk losing structural integrity. A well at Bryan Mound failed without warning in May 2024 and lost an estimated 400,000 barrels. And Sandia National Laboratories, the reserve's longtime geotechnical adviser, concluded in late 2024 that well deformation is outpacing DOE's ability to fix it at current funding levels. Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said the immediate priority is to "finish the repairs on the Strategic Petroleum Reserve."
The $20 Billion Problem
The exchanges are DOE's answer to the money question. They bring barrels back without a check from Congress. But they only bring back what was lent, plus the premium.
The reserve entered the war at about 415 million barrels. If all 172 million borrowed barrels come back with roughly 40 million barrels of interest on top, it lands somewhere around 455 million. That's our own back-of-the-envelope estimate, it assumes everything goes right, and it still leaves the reserve at only about two-thirds of the roughly 680 million barrels DOE says the system can effectively hold.
Getting the rest of the way means buying oil. DOE has estimated it would cost about $20 billion to buy the roughly 250 million barrels needed to get back to that effective peak, at prices near $80 a barrel. Congress set aside $171 million for crude purchases in last year's reconciliation law, enough for about 2 million barrels. As of May, DOE had spent it on a single contract for 1 million barrels.
The administration has floated refilling with Venezuelan crude, an idea that dovetails with Washington's growing stake in Venezuela's oil fields. The problem is chemistry. Orinoco crude has an API gravity of 9.5 to 12 degrees, and Venezuela's main export grade, Merey 16, sits at 16. DOE told Congress back in 2016 that it doesn't store anything heavier than 22.3 API because the operational headaches outweigh the benefits.
So "no cost to taxpayers" holds up for the exchange barrels. For the reserve as a whole, it's optimistic. Somebody eventually has to pay to fill the rest, and that bill doesn't show up anywhere in the current budget.
